name: Ephedrine / ECA stack

lead: ECA stands for ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin. It has long been popular with bodybuilders cutting fat before competitions, and a looksmax.org guide describes it as a stack for raising metabolism, suppressing appetite and adding energy.

Ephedrine triggers release of norepinephrine, activating adrenergic receptors, and also slows gastric emptying; caffeine and related compounds are reported to act synergistically with it. A 2021 systematic review found ephedrine, with or without caffeine, produced about 2 kg more weight loss than placebo over 4 to 24 weeks. Long-term effects are unknown.

paras: Users take it during cutting phases alongside a calorie deficit and training, often for limited stretches. Guides pair it with exercise for a leaner physique, and effects on appetite and energy are felt the same day.

Reported effects include insomnia, anxiety, tremor, rapid heart rate, arrhythmias and hypertension; stroke and heart attack are serious risks, and a forum guide itself warns against use with heart problems. The FDA banned ephedrine alkaloid supplements in 2004, and legal status varies by country.

angle.text: Bodybuilders and looksmaxxers use the ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin stack to raise metabolism and curb appetite when cutting, leading to fat loss and a leaner physique. Trials have found modest short-term fat loss.

lead: The ECA stack combines ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin. It is used as a cutting aid: people take it to suppress appetite, raise energy for training and burn more fat so the face and physique look leaner. It has long been popular with bodybuilders cutting fat before competitions.[1][2]

Ephedrine is a sympathomimetic stimulant that works mainly by triggering norepinephrine release. A 2021 systematic review reported about 2 kg more weight loss than placebo over 4 to 24 weeks with ephedrine, with or without caffeine; long-term effects are unknown.[1] An earlier 2003 meta-analysis in JAMA reached a similar conclusion, describing modest short-term weight loss and noting that no trial lasted longer than six months.[3]

On looksmax.org and T Nation the stack is described as an appetite suppressant that also gives enough energy for long cardio sessions and lifting while in a calorie deficit. Forum guides pair this with warnings about heart rate and heart conditions, and its legal status varies widely by country.[2][4][5]

Ephedrine has a long documented history, from the Chinese herb ma huang to its synthesis in 1885, and a prominent regulatory one: after a wave of 1990s and early-2000s supplement sales and a series of publicised deaths, the US Food and Drug Administration banned ephedrine alkaloid supplements in 2004.[1][6] Today the compound circulates in appearance and physique communities mainly as a pharmacy or imported product, and its availability differs by country.[1]

Appetite suppression, energy, fat loss while cutting

paras: In looksmaxxing and physique communities ECA is used in cutting phases, when the aim is to lower body fat while keeping muscle. The appearance payoff is the one familiar from any fat-loss phase: a leaner face with a more visible jaw and cheekbones, and clearer muscle separation.[2][4]

Posters describe three attractions: less hunger while eating in a deficit, more drive for cardio and lifting sessions, and a modest rise in energy expenditure. A looksmax.org guide lists the three components and when each is helpful, and a second guide pitches an ephedrine and caffeine stack as an appetite suppressant that supports an hour of cardio followed by weights.[2][4]

Outside forums, the same pairing has a long record in bodybuilding, where competitors have used it to cut fat before shows, and in the pre-2004 over-the-counter diet-supplement market, where ephedra extracts were commonly sold together with caffeine-containing herbs.[1][6][7]

subs.h: Ma huang and the synthesis of ephedrine
paras: The plant source, ma huang (Ephedra sinica), has been used in traditional Chinese medicine for more than 2,000 years, and appears in Chinese records from the Han dynasty as an antiasthmatic and stimulant. Other Ephedra species were brewed as 'Mormon tea' by Native Americans and Mormon pioneers.[1][6]

The Japanese chemist Nagai Nagayoshi first synthesised ephedrine in 1885. Merck began marketing it in the 1920s as ephetonin, Chinese exports to the West rose sharply between 1926 and 1928, and ephedrine entered US medical use in 1926. It later appeared in nasal products such as a 1948 decongestant nose drop.[1]

In the 1990s ephedra extracts became a mass-market dietary supplement. The best-selling brand, Metabolife 356, was first sold to bodybuilders and re-marketed as a diet aid in 1995; sales reached hundreds of millions of dollars a year.[7] In 1997 the FDA proposed limits on products with 8 mg or more of ephedrine alkaloids per serving, which industry groups opposed, and the agency withdrew the proposal in 2000.[6]

The Metabolife company later became the subject of a congressional investigation, which reported that it had received thousands of adverse-event complaints and had not passed them to regulators. Its co-founder Michael Ellis was sentenced in 2008 to six months in federal prison for lying to the FDA, and the company entered Chapter 11 in 2005.[6][7]

subs.h: Deaths, the ban and the court cases
paras: A 2000 review in the New England Journal of Medicine by Haller and Benowitz reported cases of sudden cardiac death and severe disability, many in young adults who used labelled amounts of ephedra products.[6] The 2003 JAMA meta-analysis by Shekelle and colleagues found 2.2 to 3.6 times higher odds of psychiatric, autonomic or gastrointestinal symptoms and of palpitations with ephedra or ephedrine, and found no trials of athletic performance.[3]

On 16 February 2003 the Baltimore Orioles pitcher Steve Bechler, 23, collapsed during spring-training conditioning and died the next day. The Broward County medical examiner listed several contributors, among them a pre-existing liver condition, mild hypertension, heat and humidity, low food intake and ephedra toxicity; the examiner said ephedra had played a significant role.[6][8] Baseball's commissioner called for a ban, and Congress dropped its resistance to FDA action.[6][8]

The FDA warned consumers on 30 December 2003 and issued a final rule banning ephedrine alkaloid supplements on 12 April 2004.[6] In April 2005 a federal judge in Utah ruled that the agency had not shown low doses to be unsafe; the Tenth Circuit reinstated the ban on 17 August 2006, and the Supreme Court declined to hear the case in May 2007.[1][6] The Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act, signed on 6 March 2006, added sales limits and record-keeping for ephedrine and pseudoephedrine products.[1]

Ephedrine indirectly activates alpha and beta adrenergic receptors via norepinephrine release, raising blood pressure, heart rate and contractility. Animal studies show it stimulates thermogenesis in brown fat; adult humans have little brown fat, so heat production is thought to occur mainly in skeletal muscle. It also slows gastric emptying.[1] Caffeine and theophylline have a synergistic effect with ephedrine for weight loss.[1]

Caffeine on its own is described in sports-medicine literature as an ergogenic aid that can let athletes train at a greater power output or for longer.[9] Aspirin is the third component of the stack; forum posters add it for its blood-thinning effect.[4]

Medically, ephedrine is used mainly to prevent low blood pressure during anaesthesia, and it has been used for asthma and narcolepsy. Onset is within 15 to 60 minutes by mouth, and effects last roughly two to four hours.[1]

A 2021 systematic review found that ephedrine at the studied doses, with or without caffeine, over 4 to 24 weeks produced about 2 kg more weight loss than placebo. It also raised heart rate and HDL, lowered LDL and did not significantly change blood pressure.[1]

The 2003 JAMA meta-analysis screened 530 articles and pooled controlled trials of ephedrine alone, ephedrine plus caffeine and ephedra herbal products. It reported additional weight loss of roughly 0.6 to 1.0 kg per month compared with placebo, about 1.0 kg per month for ephedrine plus caffeine, and noted that no weight-loss trial exceeded six months.[3] The authors concluded that ephedrine and ephedra promote modest short-term weight loss.[3]

A general encyclopedia account of weight-loss supplements states that herbal products have not been shown to be effective and that dietary supplements lack clinical evidence of efficacy for weight loss.[10] Physique-community posters point to the stack's effect on appetite and training energy rather than to the scale alone.[2][4]

Common effects include insomnia, anxiety, headache, nausea, dizziness, tremor and dry mouth. Cardiovascular effects include tachycardia, arrhythmias and hypertension, and serious risks include stroke and heart attack. Psychiatric effects can include agitation and, rarely, mania or hallucinations. Combining it with MAO inhibitors can cause hypertensive crisis.[1] A review of drug-induced kidney stones lists ephedrine-containing preparations among the drugs that can cause them at high or long-term exposure.[11]

By 2004 the FDA had received more than 18,000 adverse-effect reports linked to ephedrine products.[1] A 2003 study in Annals of Internal Medicine found ephedrine alkaloid products were 100 to 700 times more likely to cause a significant adverse reaction than kava or ginkgo.[6] Metabolife 356 was reported in a clinical trial to raise blood pressure and cause mild arrhythmias, and ephedra supplements were linked to more than 100 deaths.[7]

Looksmax.org guides themselves caution against use by people with heart problems, say the stack is not meant for people who do not exercise, and tell users to track resting heart rate and avoid high-intensity intervals while on it.[2][4]

In 2004 the FDA banned ephedrine alkaloids marketed for purposes other than asthma, colds, allergies or traditional Asian use; a Utah federal court ruled against the rule in 2005 and the Tenth Circuit upheld it in 2006.[1] Ephedrine is prescription-only in Australia and Germany (the latter since April 2006), restricted in Canada, and is a UN Table I precursor because it can be used to make methamphetamine.[1] Ephedra extracts that contain no ephedrine alkaloids remain legal in the US.[6] The looksmax.org ECA guide says availability depends on national law.[2]

Ephedrine is banned by WADA and the IOC and by the NCAA, NFL, NBA and MLB. High-profile sport cases include Diego Maradona's positive test at the 1994 World Cup.[1][6] A 2006 survey reported that nearly half of collegiate hockey players had used ephedra.[6]

One looksmax.org guide pitches an ephedrine and caffeine stack as an appetite killer that supports prolonged cardio, and a longer ECA guide lists the three components and when each is helpful.[2][4] Replies in the ECA thread debate which kind of exercise suits fat loss.[2]

A 17-year-old poster described running ephedrine and caffeine to 'leanmaxx' and asked about adding the growth hormone secretagogue MK-677, reasoning that ephedrine would blunt the hunger MK-677 causes; a reply cautioned that a calorie deficit could work against muscle and bone growth.[12]

On T Nation, lifters describe ephedrine as part of cutting routines. One user lists an ECA stack alongside carnitine, caffeine, yohimbine and very low calories, another says he monitors resting heart rate while using the EC stack, and another says the only cutting supplements that really worked were ephedrine products sold before the US ban.[13][14][15]

ECA belongs to a wider family of thermogenic or 'fat burner' supplements that combine caffeine with other stimulants, and sits beside other cutting tools discussed in the same communities, such as caffeine-only stacks, carnitine and yohimbine.[13][10] It is also discussed next to growth-hormone secretagogues, as in the MK-677 thread.[12] Wikipedia's coverage of looksmaxxing situates the community within 2010s online forums and its later spread to TikTok and streaming platforms.[16]

Trials of ephedrine with or without caffeine for weight loss have been pooled in a 2021 systematic review, which reported about 2 kg greater loss than placebo over 4 to 24 weeks, and in the 2003 JAMA meta-analysis described above, which also catalogued adverse events from 52 controlled trials and 65 case reports.[1][3] A 2000 NEJM review compiled reports of cardiovascular events.[6] No studies were found on the ECA stack specifically for cosmetic or looksmaxxing outcomes.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org and T Nation, ECA is presented as a cutting stack for appetite suppression and energy, with recurring warnings about heart health and with nostalgia among some lifters for products sold before the US ban.[2][4][15]
